source.title: Identifying Interpretable Subspaces in Image Representations
source.authors: N. Kalibhat; S. Bhardwaj; C. Bruss; Hamed Firooz; Maziar Sanjabi; S. Feizi

record.tranche_reason: The study reports that only a small portion of image-model representation spaces is explainable through individual features, and that feature groups can be more interpretable. This qualifies claims about individual-neuron interpretability, though it does not test the language-model pole audit or the essay’s proposed causes.
record.gate_note: The paper studies image-model features, not neuron poles in language models. It does not test Qwen3-32B, the InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, language-model scales, attribution graphs, or explanation scoring on new text. Its reported human evaluations of concept quality and comparisons with other explanation methods do not directly measure the claim versions. Table A.3 has model-specific figures, but its flattened layout does not support assigning all values reliably; the paper’s prose gives the aggregate estimate used here.
record.test_reason: With a modern automated tool (FALCON), the paper reports that under 20% of final-layer features in ResNet-50 vision models are candidates for individual explanation. It says most remaining late-layer features activate unrelated images. This bears on V4's claim that late-layer vision neurons become largely interpretable with better tools. It does not test V4's causal account (architecture, regularization) or any language-model version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors propose FALCON, a CLIP+LAION captioning framework with contrastive filtering, to explain vision-model features. They report that under about 20% of final-layer representation space is explainable by individual features, while feature groups are more interpretable and cover more of the space. They also apply the concepts to debugging misclassifications and transfer them across models with a linear map.
record.recipe_differences: FALCON explains image-model features by captioning highly activating image crops, ranking concepts, and filtering them using low-activation images; this is not the essay’s neuron-pole audit or the original language-model explanation-and-testing method.
record.method_sensitivity: The high-activation threshold α is selected according to each representation space’s distribution. The paper also describes feature-group selection using a CLIP cosine-similarity threshold γ. It notes that the models have differing numbers of highly activating or interpretable features/groups.

fits_no_version.finding: Groups of final-layer features activate more coherent image sets than single features (e.g. DINO features 763+1927 give morel mushroom textures). Interpretable-group counts per model: 91–293.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In vision-model final layers, concepts are often encoded jointly by small groups of neurons rather than by single neurons.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), PMLR 202, 2023
record.problems: The candidate share is based on a high-activation threshold, which the paper says does not guarantee explainability. The study concerns vision representations and does not test the language-model audit or the proposed causal explanation involving architecture, regularization, and tool quality. No uncertainty estimates are stated for the aggregate share.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows omitted. Model-specific Table A.3 values were not transcribed because the supplied flattened table layout does not reliably support assigning every value to its model.

missing.what: Per-model share of final-layer features with more than 10 highly activating samples (α in parentheses): ResNet-50 supervised 0.68% (0.27), SimCLR 21.92% (0.34), MoCo 17.70% (0.34), DINO 16.66% (0.14), BYOL 25.63% (0.24), SimSiam 8.00% (0.32), SwaV 6.00% (0.31). The flattened table is readable in column order.
Qualitative statement that features outside the threshold, or under relaxed α, 'do not activate a resembling set of images'. Examples in Figures 4 and A.3 (DINO ResNet-50).

record.verdict_notes: The study is in vision models, not language models, so it bears only on V4. Its 'explainable' share is an activation-frequency selection criterion at α = mean + 16×std, not a human-judged interpretability rate, and it depends on α. The human precision and recall (about 0.86/0.84) apply only to features that were already selected. Not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B audit and its shares of one-job, two-related-job, and not-yet-understood poles.
Language models, dense versus mixture-of-experts models, and scaling up to trillions of parameters.

The InceptionV1-sized model estimates, the proposed 5% to 99% change, and whether architecture, regularization, or tool quality causes changes in interpretability.
Attribution graphs, reconstruction error, and whether a replacement model is needed.
Whether explanations fit activating examples but fail to predict activation on new text.
Automated explanation scores on new text and the share of neurons reaching good scores.

relationships.condition: Final-layer features of ResNet-50 vision models (supervised and self-supervised), explained with a 2023 CLIP-based tool (FALCON) at a strict activation threshold
relationships.reason: Only about 0.7–26% of features (supervised ResNet-50 0.68%) even qualify for individual explanation (R1, Table A.3). The paper says most others activate unrelated images, so a better tool alone does not make late-layer neurons mostly interpretable here. The share is a threshold-dependent upper bound, not a judged rate.
relationships.display_finding: Only about 0.7–26% of features qualified for individual explanation, 0.68% for supervised ResNet-50, and most others activated on unrelated images, so the newer tool did not make late-layer features mostly interpretable. The share is a threshold-dependent upper bound, not a judged rate.

relation.reason: By verdict_rules section 1, a study tests a claim when its own results bear on whether a version holds. The Table A.3 and Section 3 results do bear on V4.

tranche.reason: Its own results (at most about 26% of final-layer ResNet-50 features qualify with a 2023 tool, and the rest activate diverse images) show that V4's high-share picture is partial here. That fits T5 and matches the limits_scope verdict.

source_check.notes: Only the final layer is measured, and the share is a threshold-based candidate count (alpha = mean + 16 std), not a judged rate. The paper's main claim is that feature groups, not single features, explain most of the space. That points further against neuron-level cleanliness. Table A.3 is garbled by extraction: the values and alphas pair up in model order.

statements.correction: Context only, no defect: Table A.3 gives 0.68% (supervised) to 25.63% (BYOL) of final-layer features with more than 10 samples above alpha = mean(H) + 16 std(H). The paper summarizes this as roughly 20%. It says thresholding alone does not guarantee explainability, and that feature groups explain a much larger part of the space.
0.68% = supervised ResNet-50 share of final-layer features with more than 10 samples above alpha (Table A.3). The statement correctly calls it share-like.
Supports the issue: across all Table A.3 models at most 25.63% of features qualify, and the text says the remaining features do not activate a resembling set of images.

Alpha is set per representation space (alpha = mean(H) + 16 std(H)), so Table A.3 alpha varies from 0.14 to 0.34. Supervised ResNet-50 is 0.68% at alpha 0.27. The paper says roughly 20% overall and that thresholding alone does not guarantee explainability.
